title: Associate Exam
description: A fixed 40-question exam drawn at random from a 46-question bank covering all five modules. Pass mark is 80%. This is an open-book exam — take your time, browse any module to refresh your memory, or ask the AI assistant for help. Your answers are saved as you go, so leaving the page to look something up is fine. Explanations show after submission so you can learn from any answers you missed.

questions.scenario: Business users ask IT to write SQL for every new report because the database's names, such as CUSTOMER_W_TER and PRICEEACH, mean nothing to them.
questions.prompt: What would a PME metadata domain change for them?
options: IT writes each report's SQL once in PME, and users rerun it
Each report keeps its own list of friendly names for the columns
They pick business-named fields, and the model generates the SQL
PME renames the database's tables and columns to business terms
questions.explanation:
A **metadata domain** translates technical database names into business terms, and the query generator uses the model's relationships to build the SQL, so users report by picking **business-named fields** without writing any.

The friendly names live once in the model rather than in every report, which keeps them consistent.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Getting Started — Components

questions.scenario: A DBA renames a database column that 40 reports use. All 40 reports are built on a published metadata domain.
questions.prompt: Where does the fix go?
options: In the domain's physical layer, once, then republish the domain
In each of the forty reports, which name the database column
In the business view, by adding the renamed column to each category
Nowhere, since the published domain follows the rename by itself
questions.explanation: The **metadata layer** acts as a buffer between the source data and the reports. Because reports reference business columns rather than the physical database columns, a change at the database level is absorbed in the **physical layer** of the domain. Once the physical layer is updated and the domain is republished, the reports are untouched, because their business columns have not changed.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Getting Started — Components

questions.scenario: A new modeler opens a domain. One part of the tree holds connections, physical tables, and physical columns, while another part holds business tables, relationships, and categories.
questions.prompt: Which part do report writers work against?
options: The business model layer, through its business view
The connection, through the database's own names
Both layers, choosing per column which name to show
The physical layer, through its physical columns
questions.explanation: Report writers work against the **business model layer** because it provides a business-oriented view of the data. This layer uses categories to present information in a way that applications and users can easily interact with, abstracting the technical details of the underlying database.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Getting Started — Components

questions.scenario: Dates appear as 2004-03-15 in some reports and as 15/03/2004 in others, and currency appears with and without a dollar sign. Each report author formats values by hand.
questions.prompt: What does moving the formatting into the metadata domain achieve?
options: Formatting rules written into the database's column definitions
Faster queries, as the database returns values already formatted
Formats stored with each report rather than with the data source
One set of formatting rules that every report built on it uses
questions.explanation:
Moving formatting to the metadata layer ensures that a single set of **formatting rules** for text, dates, and numbers is established within the model.

Because these rules are defined centrally in the metadata domain, every report built upon that model automatically shares the same consistent formatting for its data fields.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Getting Started — Components

questions.scenario: A global company wants one domain for all its countries. German users must see labels for their own regional settings, and salary figures must be hidden from most staff.
questions.prompt: Which two PME capabilities does that rely on?
options: The Query Editor
Calculated columns
Security controls
Localization
Complex joins
questions.explanation:
The requirement to adapt labels based on regional settings is met by **Localization**, which ensures information is presented correctly according to local context.

**Security controls** manage which data elements, such as salary figures, are visible to specific users, allowing a single domain to serve a diverse, global user base.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Getting Started — Components

questions.scenario: Three report authors, all fluent in SQL, write every company report directly against the database. A manager proposes building a metadata domain first.
questions.prompt: What is the fairest assessment of the proposal?
options: An end to database upkeep, since the domain absorbs every change
No extra upkeep at all, since the domain is generated from the database
Faster queries, as the domain caches every result, at no upkeep cost
One shared model of names, formats and security, which must be maintained
questions.explanation: A metadata domain provides a **shared model** where business names, formatting, and security are defined in one location. While this design ensures consistency across all reports and allows the system to absorb many database changes, the domain itself requires maintenance to remain in sync with the physical layer.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Getting Started — Components

questions.scenario: A domain has been designed and saved in the Metadata Editor. Report writers using Interactive Reporting cannot find it as a data source.
questions.prompt: What makes it available to them?
options: Exporting it as an XMI file into each writer's home folder
Re-importing its tables through the database connection
Saving it again, since File > Save also updates the server
Publishing it to the Pentaho Server from Metadata Editor
questions.explanation: **File > Publish To Server** sends the domain to the **Pentaho Server**, which registers it as a data source for the reporting tools. Saving the domain only stores it locally, so it never reaches the server.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — OrdersME

questions.scenario: A connection has just been imported into a new domain. The physical layer lists the database's tables and columns under their database names.
questions.prompt: What is the next step toward something report writers can use?
options: Publish it, since report writers can browse the physical layer directly
Create categories over the physical columns, then publish the domain
Build a business model whose business tables reference the physical ones
Drop the tables the reports will not need from the database itself
questions.explanation:
The **physical layer** represents the database as it is and is not part of the business model; the business tables, relationships, and business view built on top of it are what applications and users work against.

Report writers do not browse the physical layer. Because **categories** hold business columns, a business model must exist before there is anything to categorize. Unneeded tables can simply be left out of the model; no items are dropped from the actual database.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — Overview

questions.scenario: A business model must join order data in a MySQL warehouse with customer data in a separate Oracle CRM.
questions.prompt: What stops it from being built as described?
options: Relationships can join only tables of similar size.
A domain can hold only one business model at a time.
A business model can reference only one connection.
Oracle tables cannot be imported into Metadata Editor.
questions.explanation: A **business model** can reference only one connection. Because tables from different connections cannot be mixed in the same model, the data must be moved into a single database before the business model is created.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — Overview

questions.scenario: Budget figures and actual sales sit in two tables with no foreign key between them in the database. Analysts want to compare the two in one report.
questions.prompt: How can the business layer support that?
options: A relationship between the two business tables on columns they share
The two tables imported through two connections in the same model
A foreign key added in the database first, as PME follows only those
One category holding both tables' columns, which joins them for reports
questions.explanation: The business layer allows the creation of a **relationship** between two business tables based on shared columns. This enables the comparison of data across different tables even when a formal foreign key does not exist in the physical database schema.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — Overview

questions.scenario: Order Date should appear under both an Orders heading and a Time heading in a model's business view.
questions.prompt: Can the business view display the field in both locations?
options: Yes, as a column can sit in several categories, once in each
Only if both categories draw on the same business table
No, as each business column can belong to one category only
Only by creating a second business table over the same table
questions.explanation:
A business column can be added to more than one **category** in a business view. The only restriction is that a column cannot appear more than once within a single category.

Because categories are not tied to specific business tables, a column can be shared across multiple categories without requiring additional tables or duplicate entries.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — Overview

questions.scenario: A modeler imported all 40 tables of a schema into a domain's physical layer. The reporting model requires only six of those tables.
questions.prompt: What should happen to the other 34 tables?
options: They must be dropped from the database before the domain is published.
They must move to a second connection, so the model stays valid.
They must join the business model, or the domain will not validate.
They can stay, as only what a model uses reaches report writers.
questions.explanation:
The physical layer is not part of the business model, because not every table in it is needed by every model. Report writers see only the **business view**, so the unused tables are harmless and can be removed later if wanted.

Nothing requires every physical table to appear in a model, and PME never needs tables dropped from the database.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — Overview

questions.scenario: Reports need a line total, the quantity ordered multiplied by the price of each item. The ORDERDETAILS table stores only `QUANTITYORDERED` and `PRICEEACH`.
questions.prompt: How is the total provided in the domain?
options: A column PME adds to the database table when the domain is published
A calculated column with the formula [QUANTITYORDERED]*[PRICEEACH]
A calculated column with the formula {QUANTITYORDERED}*{PRICEEACH}
A relationship joining ORDERDETAILS to itself on PRICEEACH
questions.explanation: A column that does not exist in the physical table can be created as a **calculated column** using existing fields. The formula utilizes **square brackets** to identify the columns, such as `[QUANTITYORDERED]*[PRICEEACH]`.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — SteelWheels

questions.scenario: A domain built against a development database will also be published to a production server. The team wants the same domain to work on both environments without editing the domain.
questions.prompt: Which connection setup supports that?
options: JNDI access, so each server supplies the database behind one name
Two connections in the one model, one for each environment
Native JDBC, with the production host typed in before each publish
A second business model for production, with its own connection
questions.explanation: Using **JNDI access** allows the connection to name a resource, such as `SampleData`, while the application server manages the actual connection details. This configuration makes the domain portable because the specific connection details are managed by the environment's server rather than being hardcoded in the definition.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — OrdersME

questions.scenario: A relationship in the Orders model is listed as BT_ORDERS_ORDERS.BC_ORDERS_CUSTOMER_NUMBER - BT_PAYMENTS_PAYMENTS.BC_PAYMENTS_CUSTOMERNUMBER.
questions.prompt: What does it connect?
options: A business table to a physical table, Orders to Payments
Physical columns of two database tables, Orders and Payments
Business columns of two business tables, Orders and Payments
Two categories in the business view, Orders and Payments
questions.explanation: The prefix **BT** identifies a business table, and the prefix **BC** identifies a business column. Because both sides of the relationship use the **BT** and **BC** prefixes, the link connects business columns of two business tables.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — SteelWheels

questions.scenario: A modeler adds a MySQL connection in a fresh Metadata Editor install. Testing the connection fails because no driver for the database can be found.
questions.prompt: What fixes it?
options: Publishing the domain, so the server supplies the missing driver
Switching Access to JNDI and keeping the other connection settings
Copying the driver into Metadata Editor's lib folder and restarting
Copying the driver into the database server's own install folder
questions.explanation: The client tool loads the driver itself, so the **JDBC driver** goes into Metadata Editor's `lib` folder (removing any older copy of the same JAR), and the editor is restarted to register it.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — OrdersME

questions.scenario: Publishing a domain from Metadata Editor fails. Earlier that day, a user closed the Pentaho Server console window.
questions.prompt: What should be checked first?
options: That the JDBC driver is still in Metadata Editor's lib folder
That the server is running, as publishing calls its API
That every physical table appears in at least one business model
That the domain was saved as XMI into the server's own folder
questions.explanation: Publishing posts the domain to the server's **metadata import endpoint**, so the server must be running. Closing its console window stops the server, and it has to be started again before the domain can be published.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — OrdersME

questions.scenario: The OrdersME domain has been published to the Pentaho Server without errors.
questions.prompt: What best shows that report writers can actually use it?
options: Querying its tables from a database client with SQL
Re-importing the published file into Metadata Editor
Finding the XMI file among the server's solution folders
Building an Interactive Report on it in the User Console
questions.explanation: Building an Interactive Report on the domain as the data source exercises the **business view**, its categories, and the generated joins. This confirms that the metadata layer is correctly processed for end-user consumption.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — OrdersME

questions.scenario: In a star schema, ORDERFACT holds one row per order line. Each row carries a PRODUCTCODE that identifies one row of PRODUCTS.
questions.prompt: Which relationship, from ORDERFACT to PRODUCTS, describes that?
options: N:N, with PRODUCTCODE acting as the linking table
1:1, since each fact row names exactly one product
1:N, since one fact row can refer to many products
N:1, since many fact rows refer to each product
questions.explanation:
The relationship from ORDERFACT to PRODUCTS is **many-to-one (N:1)** because multiple order lines in the fact table can refer to the same single product record in the dimension table.

In a standard star schema, the fact table maintains an N:1 relationship with each of its associated dimension tables.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — OrdersME

questions.scenario: A modeler has just added relationships and aggregations to a model and wants to check them before anyone else sees it.
questions.prompt: Which tool does that inside Metadata Editor?
options: The Editor Graph, which runs the joins drawn between tables
The Query Editor, which runs a query from the categories
The Concept Editor, which previews each column's formatting
The Security Service dialog, which returns the model as XML
questions.explanation:
The **Query Editor** builds a query from business categories and columns, shows the generated SQL and the resulting data, and identifies issues with relationships, aggregations, or column definitions before deployment.

This tool allows a user to verify the logic of the metadata model by executing a query against the source data.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — Query Builder

questions.scenario: Most users of a model should see every customer, but one specific business area requires a filtered version of the same customer table.
questions.prompt: How can one model hold both?
options: Two categories over the customer columns, one of them filtered
Two business tables that reference the same physical table
A copy of the customer table made in the database for that area
Two connections to the same database, one for each business area
questions.explanation: One model can accommodate different requirements by defining **two business tables** that reference the same physical table. This allows the metadata layer to present the same source data in different ways for different business needs, such as applying specific filters or security constraints.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — Overview

questions.scenario: A new business model's ID is `BV_MODEL_1`. The modeler would like it to read OrderStarCustomer, matching the model's name.
questions.prompt: What should the modeler do?
options: Change the ID, since it is only a label shown to report writers.
Delete the ID, and Metadata Editor regenerates it from the name.
Leave the ID as it is and set the Name property instead.
Change the ID, then republish so the server picks up the new value.
questions.explanation: The **ID** is used internally to reference the model when SQL is generated and must be unique across all models. The **Name** property is the correct field for display labels that users see.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Properties — OrderStarCustomer

questions.scenario: A modeler selects four physical tables together and drags them onto a model's Business Tables, but they are not added.
questions.prompt: How are these tables added?
options: One at a time, each drag opening a properties dialog
By importing them again from the connection into the model
As a group, once the model's relationships have been defined
As a group, once a category exists for them to drop into
questions.explanation: Tables cannot be added to the business layer as a group; they must be added individually. Each drag operation triggers a **properties dialog** that displays the business table's ID (such as `BT_PRODUCTS_PRODUCTS`) and its corresponding physical table, where the user can then choose to remove specific columns.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Properties — OrderStarCustomer

questions.scenario: The physical table `PT_PRODUCTS` was dragged into a model, creating the business table `BT_PRODUCTS_PRODUCTS`. Later, a description is set on one of the physical table's columns.
questions.prompt: What happens to the matching business column?
options: Nothing, as the business table took a copy when created.
It inherits the description, unless it overrides its own.
It inherits it, replacing a description it had overridden.
It inherits it, and loses every property it had overridden.
questions.explanation:
A business table maintains a **reference link** to the physical table it models. Business columns inherit properties from their corresponding physical columns on a per-property basis.

If a property is not explicitly overridden, the business column **inherits the value** from the physical column. If a business column has its own override, that specific property remains unchanged regardless of updates to the physical column's property.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — Overview

questions.scenario: A model contains business tables for ORDERFACT, CUSTOMER_W_TER, PRODUCTS, and DIM_TIME. The tables have populated categories, but no relationships have been defined yet. A report writer plans to include Customer Name and Total in the same report.
questions.prompt: What does the model still lack for that report?
options: A relationship from ORDERFACT to CUSTOMER_W_TER for the join
A category holding both columns, which supplies their join
A shared parent concept on both columns so they line up
A calculated column that combines Customer Name and Total
questions.explanation: A **relationship** tells the query and SQL generators how business tables join. The report takes Customer Name from CUSTOMER_W_TER and Total from ORDERFACT, so the two need one, here ORDERFACT N:1 to CUSTOMER_W_TER on `CUSTOMERNUMBER`.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Properties — OrderStarCustomer

questions.scenario: A mask is set on a physical column. A different mask is then set on the business column that references it.
questions.prompt: Which mask does the business column use?
options: The physical column's, since physical metadata always wins out
Neither, since the two conflicting masks cancel each other out
Its own, since its override replaces the inherited mask
Whichever mask was set most recently, wherever it was set
questions.explanation:
A business column inherits the metadata of a physical column until a property is overridden. When an **override** is applied, the business layer uses its own specific configuration for that property.

Physical metadata acts as the default value, but the specific configuration of the business layer takes precedence over the inherited values.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Domains & Models — Overview

questions.scenario: A modeler attempts to delete the Target Table property from a physical table to tidy the property list, but the Metadata Editor does not allow the action.
questions.prompt: Why can it not be deleted?
options: It comes from the Base concept, which cannot be deleted.
It belongs to the connection, so only its owner may edit it.
It is a required property, which SQL generation depends on.
It is locked until the domain has been published once.
questions.explanation: Physical objects carry **mandatory properties** that are created automatically and cannot be deleted, so nothing essential to **SQL generation** can be removed by accident. A physical table must always have a Target Table.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Properties — Overview

questions.scenario: Reports need one Contact Name field that reads Last, First. The customer table stores `CONTACTLASTNAME` and `CONTACTFIRSTNAME` separately.
questions.prompt: How is the field built in the domain?
options: A category holding both name columns, which reports show as one field
A concept with a mask that merges the two name columns into one
A physical column with a joining formula, added to the business table
A relationship between the two name columns of the customer table
questions.explanation: A new **physical column** (`PC_CONTACT`) takes the formula `[CONTACTLASTNAME]+","+[CONTACTFIRSTNAME]` and is then added to the business table, so it can be categorized like any other column.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Properties — OrderStarCustomer

questions.scenario: Report writers see fields named `PRODUCTCODE` and `CUSTOMERNUMBER` in a published data source.
questions.prompt: What gives them Product Code and Customer Number instead?
options: Putting the columns in categories named for the business labels
Setting a concept on each column that turns its name into a label
Overriding each business column's Name property with the label
Renaming the columns in the database, then importing them again
questions.explanation:
Overriding the **Name property** of each business column with the business label is what report writers then see.

The label lives in the metadata layer, so the database columns keep their names.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Properties — OrderStarCustomer

questions.scenario: Report writers summarizing Price Sold usually want a sum. Sometimes they want the average, the smallest, or the largest instead.
questions.prompt: How is Price Sold set up to allow all of these?
options: Four calculated columns, one for each of the aggregations wanted
Default Aggregation Sum, with the others written into each report
Default Aggregation Sum, with Average, Minimum and Maximum optional
No aggregation set, so that the report tool chooses one each time
questions.explanation: **Default Aggregation** sets the aggregation applied when nobody chooses one (Sum), and **Optional Aggregations** lists the others report writers may pick, here Average, Minimum, and Maximum.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Properties — OrderStarCustomer

questions.scenario: ORDERFACT is joined N:1 to CUSTOMER_W_TER with an Inner join. A few order rows carry a CUSTOMERNUMBER that is missing from the customer table.
questions.prompt: What happens to those rows in a report using both tables?
options: They appear with blank customer columns, as unmatched rows are kept.
They are left out, since an inner join keeps only matched rows.
They appear once for every customer, as the join cannot match them.
They make the report fail until the missing customers are added.
questions.explanation: An **inner join** produces a result only where there is a match in both tables based on the join condition. When a row in one table does not have a corresponding match in the other table, that row is excluded from the final result set.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Properties — OrderStarCustomer

questions.scenario: Forty currency columns across several models each carry their own copy of the same mask. Finance requires negative values to be displayed in parentheses.
questions.prompt: What setup would make a change like this a single edit?
options: A USCurrency concept set as the parent of every currency column
The mask set on each physical column instead of each business one
The mask set on each category that holds currency columns
A calculated column for each currency field that formats it as text
questions.explanation: A **concept** bundles properties once, and columns inherit them. With the concept set as the parent of the currency columns, one change to its mask reaches every one of them.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Concepts — Concept Editor

questions.scenario: A USCurrency concept exists in the Concept Editor, but Price Sold in the Orders category still shows plain numbers.
questions.prompt: What action links the column to the concept?
options: Typing USCurrency into the column's Mask for Number or Date
Dragging Price Sold onto USCurrency in the Concept Editor
Right-clicking Price Sold and choosing Set Parent Concept
Adding USCurrency to the Orders category's properties
questions.explanation: A column inherits a concept's properties only once the concept is assigned to it. Right-clicking the column and choosing **Set Parent Concept** links the two, and the column then takes the formatting defined in the **Concept Editor**.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Concepts — Concept Editor

questions.scenario: Some physical columns should stop picking up the default properties of the Base concept. A modeler considers deleting Base from the concept list.
questions.prompt: What does Metadata Editor allow?
options: Deleting Base, once every column has been given another parent
Deleting Base, so that columns fall back to the database's formats
Removing Base as those columns' parent, while Base itself stays
Nothing, as Base's properties can be neither changed nor removed
questions.explanation:
Base can be removed as the parent of particular columns, so they stop inheriting its properties, but the **Base concept** itself cannot be deleted from the concept list.

Base's own properties can still be updated, added, or deleted.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Concepts — Overview

questions.scenario: A business column has a mask typed directly onto it in the editor. Its parent concept is USCurrency, which sits beneath Number.
questions.prompt: Which level of concept does the directly typed mask belong to?
options: The parent concept
The self-concept
An inherited concept
The default concept
questions.explanation:
Properties applied directly to an object are its **self-concept**, so a mask typed onto the column belongs there.

USCurrency is the column's **parent concept**, Number an **inherited concept** further up the hierarchy, and Base the **default concept**, which supplies any value not set elsewhere.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Concepts — Overview

questions.scenario: Employee Number must not appear in report writers' column lists. When it is read, it must show as a whole number.
questions.prompt: Which parent concept fits this requirement?
options: ID, whose # mask shows the value as a whole number in reports
Hidden, a child of ID that also sets Hidden For the User?
USCurrency, with its mask overridden to # on the column
Number, with its mask overridden to # on the column
questions.explanation: The **Hidden** concept inherits the `#` mask from its parent, **ID**, so the value shows as a whole number, and it adds **Hidden For the User?**, which drops the column from report interfaces.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Concepts — Concept Editor

questions.scenario: All dates in reports must appear as MM-dd-yyyy. The Order Date, Required Date, and Shipped Date are all affected.
questions.prompt: How is this set up?
options: A Date concept under Number, inheriting its #,##0 mask unchanged
A Date concept with the mask MM-dd-yyyy, set as each column's parent
The MM-dd-yyyy mask typed once into the Orders category's properties
A Date concept under USCurrency, keeping its currency mask for dates
questions.explanation:
A **Date concept** is created under Base with the mask set to `MM-dd-yyyy` and then assigned as the parent of each specific date column to ensure consistent formatting across the report.

By defining the format at the **concept level**, the requirement is met for all columns sharing that underlying definition.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Concepts — Concept Editor

questions.scenario: The `USCurrency` concept sits beneath the `Number` concept and overrides only the mask property. The text alignment of the `Number` concept is later changed from Right to Left.
questions.prompt: What happens to columns whose parent is `USCurrency`?
options: They stay right-aligned, as `USCurrency` copied `Number` when it was created.
They lose their currency mask, as `Number`'s change resets its children.
They align left too, as `USCurrency` inherits alignment from `Number`.
They stay right-aligned until each column's parent is set again.
questions.explanation:
Inheritance is **live**; a child concept inherits every property from its parent except those it specifically overrides. Because the `USCurrency` concept only overrides the mask, it continues to inherit the alignment property from the `Number` parent.

Since the property is inherited dynamically, the columns update to the new alignment immediately without requiring the parent to be reassigned.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Concepts — Concept Editor

questions.scenario: Order Date and Required Date both have the Date concept as their parent. In a report, Order Date shows as 03-15-2004, but Required Date still appears as stored text.
questions.prompt: What explains the difference?
options: Required Date sits in a different category to Order Date
The Date concept formats the first date in a category only
Only Order Date's Data Type was overridden to Date
Required Date's parent concept was set after publishing
questions.explanation:
The **Mask for Number or Date** applies only to fields specifically defined as date or numeric data types. Because the Order Date was explicitly overridden to a date type while Required Date remained a string, only the former is formatted by the system.

Formatting logic is applied based on the individual field's **Data Type** definition rather than the grouping or category in which the field resides.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Concepts — Concept Editor

questions.scenario: A modeler proposes creating USCurrency directly under Base and copying Number's right alignment into it, instead of nesting it under Number.
questions.prompt: What is the fairest assessment of the proposal?
options: It is better, since a nested concept cannot override a parent's mask
It is needed, since a concept can have only one level of children
It works, but alignment is then kept in two places instead of one
It makes no difference, since concepts copy their parent when created
questions.explanation:
Nesting a concept allows it to **inherit properties** from a parent while only defining specific differences. If the modeler copies the alignment into a top-level concept, it works, but the value must be updated in two locations if the alignment needs to change.

Using a **nested hierarchy** ensures that common properties are managed in a single location, which reduces maintenance and the risk of inconsistency.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Concepts — Concept Editor

questions.scenario: Sales representatives in the Power User role build reports on a customer domain. They must not see the Credit Limit field, while the Admin role must have access to it.
questions.prompt: Where is the restriction set?
options: On the Credit Limit business column, assigning Metadata Security to Admin
On the customer business table, as a role-based row data constraint
In the database, as a view without Credit Limit for the sales reps
In the Customers category, by removing Credit Limit from it entirely
questions.explanation:
The restriction is applied by overriding the **Metadata Security** for the Credit Limit business column. By assigning access specifically to the Admin role, the field is hidden from all other roles, including those of the sales representatives.

This approach ensures that **column-level security** is enforced in the metadata layer, removing the need to create separate database views for different user roles.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Security & Data Access — Row-Level Security

questions.scenario: EMEA sales managers must see only EMEA customers from the same domain everyone else uses. An administrator must still see all customers.
questions.prompt: Which security mechanism fits?
options: A role-based MQL data constraint on the business model
Metadata Security on the Territory column, granted to EMEA managers
A separate business model for EMEA with a connection of its own
A category named EMEA that holds only the EMEA customer columns
questions.explanation:
A **role-based MQL data constraint** on the business model filters the rows each role sees, with formulas such as `Territory = "EMEA"` for the managers' role and `TRUE()` for Administrator. A role with no entry sees no rows.

Everyone shares one domain, and **row-level security** decides what each of them gets back.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Security & Data Access — Overview

questions.scenario: A team codes its security rules into each report's query. A consultant proposes moving them into the metadata domain instead.
questions.prompt: What is the strongest reason to accept the proposal?
options: Reports can then be shared with other users without publishing them.
The database no longer needs logins or permissions of its own at all.
Rules defined once are enforced in every tool, including later reports.
Reports run faster, since a secured domain is cached for each user.
questions.explanation: Security defined in the **metadata layer** is enforced consistently by every reporting tool and data access method that queries the domain. This ensures that no report has to reimplement security logic, including reports created in the future.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Security & Data Access — Overview

questions.scenario: Suzy, a Power User, needs to use the OrderSecurity domain. The Power User role has been added to the business model's Metadata Security, but she still sees no columns.
questions.prompt: Which two further steps complete her access?
options: Renaming the model so that it shows as a new data source
Adding a data constraint for Power User on each business table
Copying metadata_security.xml into the Pentaho Server
Stopping the Metadata Security override on each category
Republishing the domain and refreshing Reporting Metadata
questions.explanation:
While model-level **Metadata Security** is inherited by business tables and columns, it is not inherited by the business view's categories. To ensure visibility, the **override** must be stopped on each category.

Security changes only take effect once the domain is **republished** and the server's **Reporting Metadata** is refreshed.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Security & Data Access — Row-Level Security

questions.scenario: In Metadata Editor, the list of users and roles offered for Metadata Security is empty, so nothing can be assigned.
questions.prompt: What has to be configured?
options: Tools > Security, pointed at the server's userrolelist
A Hidden concept for each role in the Concept Editor
The data-access roles in the server's data-access settings.xml
A JDBC connection to the server's internal user database
questions.explanation:
The Metadata Editor retrieves users, roles, and access control lists from the Pentaho Server's security service. This service is configured under **Tools > Security** with a URL, such as `http://localhost:8080/pentaho/api/userrolelist`.

On a server with hundreds of users, returning only **roles** is the practical choice.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Security & Data Access — Row-Level Security

questions.scenario: A domain is published with no security changes. An administrator can choose it as a data source, but a Power User cannot see it at all.
questions.prompt: What explains this?
options: The domain was published with a Native JDBC connection.
The Power User's row-level constraint returns no rows, hiding the domain.
By default only Administrator can use metadata domains.
The domain's column security hides every column from the Power User role.
questions.explanation: Out of the box only the authenticated **Administrator** can use metadata domains, so the Power User role has to be granted access, through the model's Metadata Security or the data-access roles in the server's `settings.xml`.
questions.source: Pentaho BI Developer - ME Associate: Security & Data Access — Row-Level Security
